headline: The Three Capabilities Remaking AI Video as a Medium
lede: A developer affiliated with the model-deployment startup fal posted a three-item shortlist — Kling's motion control, LTX-2's audio conditioning, and Wan's animate video inpainting — that functions as a diagnosis of AI video's remaining hard problems. Each addresses a different failure mode that has kept the medium feeling like a novelty rather than a production tool. The poster, Gokay Aydogan, is a well-connected open-source ML practitioner who tracks cutting-edge generative video research and has published more than sixty-five fine-tuned models.
body:
The most immediately viral of the three is *motion control* in Kling 2.6, released by Kuaishou Technology (1024.HK) in December 2025. The technique accepts a short reference video — a dancer, a martial artist, anyone in motion — and transfers its skeletal pattern onto a target character image, producing a new clip of that character performing the same movements. The system analyzes body positions, limb articulation, and timing while separately modeling mass and gravity, so a leaping character lands with plausible force and fabric responds to acceleration. Earlier Kling versions struggled with hand rendering and facial tracking under motion; version 2.6 targeted both. The result is a category of content — any character through any choreography — that previously required motion-capture rigs and compositing artists.

The more technically ambitious entry is **audio conditioning** in LTX-2, Lightricks's second-generation video model, published in January 2026. Most AI video systems generate visuals first and add audio afterward — a sequential process that produces obvious desynchronization. LTX-2 instead uses a dual-stream *diffusion transformer* in which a 14-billion-parameter video stream and a 5-billion-parameter audio stream denoise in parallel, linked by bidirectional cross-attention operating on shared time coordinates. Lip movements synchronize with speech because audio and video are generated as a coupled joint distribution rather than stitched together in postproduction. Users can independently adjust how closely each stream tracks its conditioning signal — push the audio influence higher, and the visual content follows the sound more faithfully. The model is fully open-source under Apache 2.0, a significant structural fact in a field otherwise dominated by closed APIs.

The third capability comes from Alibaba Group's (BABA) Tongyi Lab, and is less a single feature than a cluster under the Wan 2.x family. Wan2.2-Animate does what Kling's motion control does, but adds a second mode: replacing an existing character in a video with a new one while preserving background, motion, and environment — video-driven character synthesis rather than frame-by-frame editing. A related capability, *Fun Inpainting*, takes a start frame and an end frame and generates all intermediate frames as a coherent clip, filling in missing time rather than missing space. Both are released under Apache 2.0. The theoretical unification sits in VACE, a framework accepted at the *International Conference on Computer Vision* (ICCV) in 2025, which treats animation, replacement, and masked editing as variants of a single generative task.

The three choices sketch a thesis about which constraints matter most right now. *Motion control* is about authoring — giving creators deterministic leverage over what a character does rather than prompting and hoping. Audio conditioning addresses synchrony — the stubborn gap between what a clip looks like and what it sounds like. *Animate inpainting* addresses identity — placing a specific subject into or through a video sequence. As of early 2026, four of the six major AI video platforms natively generate synchronized audio, a capability that existed in none of them twelve months earlier. The field is moving from text-to-video novelty toward a toolkit that professional production can actually use.

concepts.definition: A technique that extracts movement data from a reference video — body positions, limb timing, gesture arcs — and applies that motion template to a different character or subject in a new video. The result preserves the choreography of the original while rendering it on a new visual identity, without frame-by-frame hand-animation.

A neural network architecture that generates media by iteratively denoising a random signal. Unlike earlier diffusion models built on U-Net backbones, a DiT uses transformer attention layers as its core building block, which scales more predictably with model size and handles long-range dependencies across frames or audio windows more effectively.

In generative modeling, conditioning means providing the model with additional input — here, audio signals — that shapes what it produces. In LTX-2 specifically, audio conditioning refers to joint generation: both audio and video are produced simultaneously as a coupled output, with each stream influencing the other, rather than one being generated sequentially from the other.

In statistics and machine learning, a joint distribution models the probability of two or more variables — here, audio and video — occurring together. Generating from a joint distribution means the model learns what audio-and-video combinations are realistic as a unit, so outputs are mutually consistent rather than independently sampled and then combined.

A mechanism in transformer models where two data streams — here, audio and video — each attend to information in the other simultaneously. Bidirectional means the influence flows both ways at every layer: audio shapes video representations and video shapes audio representations. This is how LTX-2 enforces temporal synchrony between the two streams.

Standard image inpainting fills in a missing or masked region within a single frame. Temporal inpainting extends this to the time dimension: given two anchor frames — a start and an end — the model generates all intermediate frames as a plausible video sequence. Wan's Fun Inpainting is an example, filling in missing time between two provided images rather than missing space within one.

A generative video framework from Alibaba's Tongyi Lab, accepted at the International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) in 2025, that unifies multiple video editing and animation tasks — animate-anything, replace-anything, expand-anything — under a single architecture. It treats character animation, masked region editing, and reference-based video generation as instances of the same conditional generation problem.

repos.summary: Official implementation of LTX-2, Lightricks's joint audio-video generation model. Contains weights for 22B and 19B variants plus a distilled version, inference code, and LoRA fine-tuning tools. Released January 2026 under Apache 2.0; notable as the first open-source model to generate synchronized audio and video from a single diffusion process.

Official repository for Alibaba Tongyi Lab's Wan 2.2 video model family, including Wan2.2-Animate and Fun Inpainting. Provides inference scripts, preprocessing pipelines for motion and pose extraction, and Apache 2.0 weights supporting both character animation and character replacement modes.

Research implementation of VACE (accepted at ICCV 2025), Alibaba's unified framework for conditional video generation. Covers animate-anything, move-anything, swap-anything, reference-anything, and expand-anything as variants of a single masked video-to-video conditional generation architecture.

fact_check: The label 'LTX-2 audio conditioning' could imply that audio drives video generation — that is, a user supplies a soundtrack and the model generates matching visuals. The released model's primary mode is actually the reverse: a text prompt simultaneously produces synchronized video and audio as a joint output (text-to-audiovisual generation). An audio-to-video pipeline exists in the codebase, but its full capability in the released weights is not confirmed by the January 2026 technical paper. The practical result — synchronized audio and video — is real and significant; the framing slightly mischaracterizes the direction of conditioning. Separately, 'Wan animate video inpainting' collapses two distinct Wan capabilities — Wan2.2-Animate for character animation and replacement, and Fun Inpainting for temporal frame interpolation — into a single term. A useful compression, but the two are separate models with different architectures.
